strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP evaluation problem: agreement across evaluator models matters alongside correlation with human judgments. The checklist framework is simple, requires no evaluator training, and provides an inspectable decomposition of each score.

Experiments cover twelve open and proprietary evaluators across two established benchmarks. Table 1 shows improved average correlations for most model–dataset combinations, including substantial gains for weaker evaluators: Llama3.1-8B improves from 0.11 to 0.46 Spearman correlation on Topical-Chat.

The presentation includes useful seed questions, prompt templates, model details, and dimension-level results. The limitations discussion appropriately acknowledges manual checklist construction and difficulties with low-quality and longer texts.
weaknesses: The central agreement claim is insufficiently specified. Section 5.2 does not explain whether CheckEval’s agreement is computed over individual binary answers or aggregate quality scores, how these are compared with Likert ratings, or which distance function is used for Krippendorff’s alpha. Agreement on binary checklist items does not directly establish agreement on final text-quality scores. The claimed 0.45 improvement and comparison with human kappa require a documented, comparable measurement protocol.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the useful appendix. The complete final checklists are absent, and augmentation prompts retain unspecified fields such as {conditions}, {constraints}, and {example}; no implementation or artifact link is provided. Because stochastic generation and filtering determine the actual evaluation instrument, seed questions and checklist counts alone cannot reconstruct the reported experiments.

The comparisons do not isolate the proposed mechanism. CheckEval simultaneously introduces more detailed criteria, binary responses, multiple judgments, and aggregation. Rubric-matched Likert scoring and seed-only checklist controls would help establish which changes produce the gains. The filtering comparison in Appendix A addresses only one component. Additionally, Section 4.4 specifies n=1 without explaining whether G-Eval’s probability-weighted scoring is reproduced, leaving the baseline implementation uncertain.

Some checklist items appear misaligned with their intended dimensions. Table 16’s groundedness questions largely assess conversational relevance, new information, and consistency with earlier utterances rather than support from the supplied knowledge fact. Table 15 rewards using the source’s terminology under relevance, potentially penalizing valid paraphrases. A targeted human audit is needed to support the claim that the checklist faithfully operationalizes benchmark criteria.

Numerical reporting and statistical analysis require correction. Table 8 reverses the Topical-Chat Pearson and Spearman means relative to Table 13. Table 11’s four MOVERScore Spearman values average to 0.5165, not the reported 0.4740. The Wilcoxon rank-sum test also ignores the pairing of results from the same evaluator models; paired comparisons and uncertainty estimates over evaluated texts would better support the significance claims. These issues do not erase the descriptive gains, but reduce confidence in their reported magnitude.

The additional reliability analyses support narrower conclusions than claimed. Table 8 measures variance of correlations across models, rather than per-input score variance. Figure 3 specifies a high-quality threshold of at least 3, while Table 4 documents a 1–3 human naturalness scale; applying that threshold within this dimension would yield constant gold ratings and undefined correlation unless an unreported transformation or grouping rule is used. Thresholds, transformations, and subset sizes need clarification. Together with the agreement and reproducibility gaps, these concerns prevent a positive Findings recommendation currently, but appear addressable within a revision cycle.
